entries.title: House Republican Men Are Behaving Badly, Endangering Their Seats And The Majority
entries.summary: Facing ethics allegations, those lawmakers who refuse to end their campaigns could face the wrath of voters in November.
entries.content:
Chuck Edwards was supposed to be the safe choice.

“He is the embodiment of mountain values who will fight for them every single day in Congress with honor and integrity,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) said in May 2022, after Edwards ousted a controversial one-term incumbent.

Four years later the North Carolina Republican faced a bipartisan rebuke from the House Ethics Committee, which recommended a rare censure motion for inappropriate behavior with young female staff.

“It’s going to be problematic for his campaign,” Tillis told reporters Monday evening.

A little after 3 a.m. Wednesday, Edwards dropped out of his reelection bid, leaving state Republican officials scramblingto find a replacement candidate.

Edwards is one of several Republican men in the House who face allegations that have put what should be reasonably safe districts in political jeopardy.

Reps. Max Miller (R-Ohio) and Cory Mills (R-Florida) are also under investigation by the Ethics Committee for, among other allegations, assaulting a woman (Mills) and domestic violence (Miller). Tony Gonzales, a three-term Republican from South Texas, resigned earlier this year after admitting to an affair with a staffer who later committed suicide. He was headed to likely defeat in a primary runoff to Brandon Herrera, who is now facing questions about demeaning comments he has posted about women.

In each instance, the lawmakers denied the allegations and, at least initially, asserted they would remain in their reelection campaigns. Republicans, already on the defensive amid President Donald Trump’s deep unpopularity, must now devote resources to defending red seats that shouldn’t be on the radar as competitive.

In 2024, Trump won all four of these districts by wide margins, ranging from almost 10 percentage points to 15 points. In the last 2024 analysis by The Cook Political Report With Amy Walter, none of these seats appeared on the chart of the roughly 70 most competitive House races in the country.

Now, all four are ranked among the three dozen toughest races for Republicans to defend in November.

Walter, the Cook report’s editor-in-chief, compared the current environment to the 2006 midterms,when Republicans lost 30 seats and the majority as President George W. Bush was mired in the Iraq war with terrible approval ratings.

“This year feels like déjà vu. … In both years: Unpopular war, Members mired in sex scandals,” she wrote.

In past midterm elections, however, these ethics-infused defeats did not tip the balance of power in the House, as the waves were so high that the majority party was largely doomed. But through mid-decade redistricting and a huge financial edge, today’s House Republicans have the type of political flood insurance their predecessors lacked.

They might be able to use these advantages to hold the majority by the narrowest of margins — unless several of these scandal-plagued seats fall to Democrats.

In 2006, Democrats padded their new majority by claiming a handful of seats in which Republican incumbents faced unique allegations.

Don Sherwood (R-Pennsylvania), who had won his previous two races with more than 80 percent of the vote, lost his race amid allegations that he had assaulted a mistress. John Sweeney (R-New York), a onetime rising star who had won his previous three races with more than 65 percent, lost after a report about a 911 call from his wife alleging an assault.

Mark Foley (R-Florida), who had won his previous two races by more than 35 percentage points each, resigned just weeks before the 2006 election amid an ethics investigation into sexually explicit conversations with teenage House pages, handing the seat to Democrats.

A few safe Republicans faced their own corruption investigations, including Tom DeLay (R-Texas), the House majority leader, and Bob Ney (R-Ohio), chair of the House Administration Committee. Both resigned midterm, and Republicans couldn’t hold on to those seats.

In 2010, Democrats lost their majority in a historic 63-seat loss that mostly centered around high unemployment and a conservative revolt against big government spending. But Bob Etheridge (D-North Carolina), who had won four straight races with more than 65 percent of the vote, stumbled, almost literally, into political trouble. A few young Republican operatives caught him leaving an evening fundraiser and, on video, asked about his policy positions.

Etheridge lunged toward them, grabbing one of them and repeatedly asked, “Who are you, who are you?” A neophyte opponent latched onto the viral video and gained attention, narrowly defeating him by 1 percentage point that fall.

In 2018, the political wave that swept Democrats back into power was foretold by Tim Murphy (R-Pennsylvania), who was so popular as a conservative anti-abortion Republican that Democrats did not field an opponent in his last two re-elections. But Murphy resigned in late 2017 after admitting to an affairwith a woman who accused him of pressuring her to get an abortion.

In early 2018, despite the district’s deep conservative lean, Conor Lamb, the Democratic candidate, won the special election to replace Murphy and established a playbook for other Democrats in tough districts for distancing themselves from the national party brand — ending with a more than 40-seat gain that November for Democrats.

In each of these cases, it’s a relatively safe bet that had the incumbent remained free of ethical challenges — or had they given their party more time to find an appropriate replacement — the party in power would have won those races.

That’s why Republicans this year pushed Gonzales to resign — and why some have tried to push Edwards and Miller to remove themselves from the November ballot.

And in Florida, Republican Reps. Mike Haridopolos and Anna Paulina Luna took the rare move to oppose an incumbent in their delegation, siding against Millsahead of the primary later this month.

“We need leaders in Congress who serve with integrity, energy, and an unwavering commitment to the people who sent them there,” the two Republicans wrote.

In addition to “other allegations,” the Ethics Committee is also reviewing the circumstances involving a second woman who got a restraining order against Mills last fall. But Trump has endorsed Mills, whose opposition could split among several Republican challengers.

Democrats believe Bale Dalton, a Navy veteran and former NASA official, provides the right contrast in November if Mills wins the nomination later this month.

Democrats are particularly bullish on defeating Miller, whose ex-father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), said that Miller posed such a danger that he moved his wife, daughter and granddaughter out of state to protect them.

“The allegations here are horrible, and it’s really disqualifying behavior,” Rep. Suzan DelBene (D-Washington), chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, told Scott MacFarlane Reports, an independent news organization covering Congress.

Miller, who won his last election by 15 points, has defended himself in a series of media appearances that only further raised alarms. Ohio law could allow Republicans to replace Miller by Monday, but that only can occur if Miller willingly steps aside, a scenario he is publicly rejecting.

“No one has told me to get off the ballot, and that’s because they know I can win,” Miller told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Monday.

Sometimes the replacement candidates come with their own political baggage, as is the case in Texas. Herrera’s recent career as an edgy YouTuber, filled with comments some consider misogyny, does not create the type of distance from Gonzales’ actions that most Republicans would prefer.

On Thursday, the DCCC added the district to its “Red to Blue” list as a designated battleground, a move that Republicans believe ignores the strong conservative lean of the district.

“All they will buy is another expensive humiliation in November,” Christian Martinez, an official with the National Republican Congressional Committee, told The Texas Tribune.

Past speakers tried to deal swiftly with transgressions to limit the exposure other caucus members faced in having to defend rogue colleagues. Foley and Murphy were pushed out in a matter of weeks. Speaker Mike Johnson, however, has been more reluctant to use his moral megaphone to push members aside, in part because his single-digit majority needs every possible vote to succeed.

In Edwards case, four years ago he was the replacement candidate himself.

Madison Cawthorn (R-North Carolina) had a high-profile single term in the House, fueled by uncorroborated stories about his escape from a car crash and his bid to attend the U.S. Naval Academy. Cawthorn alleged that many members of Congress attended parties with drugs and prostitutes, a story that lit up online and forced lawmakers to defend themselves against back home.

Led by Tillis, senior North Carolina Republicans rallied around Edwards, who made millions as a McDonald’s franchisee before serving six years in the state Senate. He was sold as the pure candidate, no controversy, narrowly defeating the young far-right ideologue in the May 2022 primary.

In its report released Monday, the Ethics Committee found that over several years Edwards showered two younger female aides with gifts, hand-written letters and other mementos that were sexual in nature.

“We seem to have a fondness for many of the same things,” he wrote to one aide. “Even where we do not, I’ll enjoy the adventure alongside you!"

His adventure ended Wednesday with his withdrawal from the election, and now North Carolina’s Republican leaders are searching for a new candidate. But Edwards will complete his current term, a sign of how much Johnson still needs his vote.

entries.title: A Capital Bikeshare Ride to Remember
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: a Capital Bikeshare pioneer, a very loud IndyCar race and a birthday boy at the National Zoo. 





THE LATEST

Capital Bikeshare challenge, accepted.

Earlier this summer, D.C. resident Andy Jarrin decided that his short jaunts on Capital Bikeshare — the region’s red rentable bikes — weren’t enough.

“I had seen people post their longest rides ever on [New York’s] Citi Bikes and Capital Bikeshare, and the rides didn’t seem that long,” he tells NOTUS. “I wondered, what is the longest distance someone could go between two stations.”

The answer took him 42 miles from a station in Largo, Maryland, to another just beyond Reston, Virginia. It took Jarrin, an energetic 26-year-old, just over four hours to finish the ride — and he didn’t stop along the way.

From what NOTUS can gather — and Capital Bikeshare tentatively confirmed — Jarrin’s ride may stand as the single longest continuous ride on a non-electric Bikeshare bike. We’re told someone rode 54.9 miles on an electric Bikeshare, a feat worthy of its own respect.

Mind you: The recognizable red bikes aren’t Tour de France-worthy steeds, though years ago another brave soul did use one to complete a triathlon. Each bike weighs some 40 pounds and has limited gears. Jarrin admits the worst part of the adventure was climbing westward from Georgetown into Arlington County on the Custis Trail.

The Capital Bikeshare network started in 2010 and has since expanded to include more than 8,000 bikes and 800 docking stations across the D.C. region. There have been more than 2.8 million rides on the bikes through June of this year. Jarrin discovered the bike network when he moved to D.C. from Miami three years ago.

“It was something new,” he says. “Everything is so car-centric back in Miami, so having so many bike lanes and bikes was a good change of pace.”

Are there any other Bikeshare challenges to come? Jarrin won’t say no, but he also thinks he’s now fully justified in graduating to the world of bike ownership. “Right now I want to get on a better bike and do long rides,” he says.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Jeanine Pirro took on the role of D.C.’s top prosecutor with two personas: a bombastic Fox News host willing to pursue politically charged issues with zeal, and a former Westchester County prosecutor and judge who wants to run a U.S. attorney’s office with a sense of normalcy. President Donald Trump’s botched Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool project put those sides at odds — and her job at risk, report NOTUS’ Jose Pagliery and Derek Hawkins.

Too fast, too furious, too f’ing loud. The National Gallery of Art studied how vibrations from the upcoming Freedom 250 Grand Prix would affect art, The Washington Post reports. The museum declined to share its specific findings, but some preservationists are concerned about the risk.

A group dubbed the “D.C. rat rangers” is walking the city’s wards by night to teach residents how to keep rodents at bay, Axios D.C. reports.

Howard University is offering buyouts to 600 employees as the school continues to face financial strain, The Chronicle of Higher Education reports. The voluntary buyouts were first offered in June to full-time faculty members or staff with at least 10 years of continuous employment — criteria that covers nearly 16% of the university’s workforce. They have until this fall to apply to the buyout program.





FROM VIRGINIA

Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced in a Washington Post op-ed that she’ll be “intervening” in the proposed $67 billion energy merger between NextEra and Dominion. That means she’ll formally request to be a party when regulators weigh the deal, which would create the world’s largest regulated electric utility.





FROM MARYLAND

A new state commission will study the deaths of at least 230 Black boys buried between 1870 and 1939 outside a juvenile facility with a documented history of abuse, The Washington Post reports.





METRO MOMENTS

Bao Li AP - 26217046150810 (7360x4912, AR: 1.50)
Happy birthday to the National Zoo’s Bao Li, who turned 5 this week. Giant pandas — they grow up so fast.

Have an image from around D.C. you want to share? A question for our reporters? An “only in D.C.” moment? Tell us about it.



SPORTS

It’s been a good summer for the Washington Spirit. On Thursday, coach Adrián González was named NWSL coach of the month for July, while forward Trinity Rodman earned player of the month honors. The 24-year-old Rodman collected five goals and an assist on the month, helping her team to a 5-1 record.

Just more than halfway through the regular season, Washington has the second-best record in the league, trailing Gotham by one point. The Spirit hosts the North Carolina Courage on Saturday night.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Reds, 6:45 p.m. (Fox 5)

WNBA: Mystics vs. Dream, 7:30 p.m. (ION)

entries.title: ‘No Idea What We’re Going to Do’
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Senate still stuck. Voters oust Ogles. Republicans practice El-Sayed’s full name. Next stop in the progressive vs. establishment battle: Hawaii. And: midterm déjà vu.





THE LATEST

We’re going to overtime: The Senate was supposed to leave town today for a long recess. But that’s not happening — there’s still a lot to be done and little time left to do it. And so a group incredibly eager to get some distance from Washington as soon as possible is forced to stick around and possibly work the weekend and into next week.

Will that be enough time? We’re still waiting to find out. The agenda remains pretty stacked with unknown outcomes — will Todd Blanche get the votes he needs to be confirmed as attorney general? He’s still short, per the official count. There’s also a fight about hemp regulations that needs to be resolved before a stopgap spending bill can be passed.

And, the Russia sanctions bill, which saw quick movement after the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham, is still awaiting action.

Or, as summed up by Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana): “I still have no idea what we’re going to do, and if we do something, when we’re going to do it.”

So it’s a lot of nail-biter Senate dealmaking action. But the real drama starts when these lawmakers get back home to voters who want answers on the agenda items they didn’t get to — the Iran war, the SAVE America Act and on and on.

Open tabs: McConnell Says He’s Been Released From Rehabilitation Facility to Recover at Home (NOTUS); Women’s Share of Top Military Promotions Plunged This Year (NYT); White House Begins Head Start Program Overhaul (NOTUS); The new fight over who gets to be ‘working class’ (Politico); Author of DNC’s 2024 “autopsy” says he concluded Gaza war hurt Harris (Axios)





From the campaign trail


Andy Ogles sent home: Republican primary voters in Tennessee’s redrawn 5th Congressional District voted out the controversial member of Congress last night. Former state Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher won the Republican nomination in what was drawn to be a safe seat for the GOP.

A few takeaways: First, it’s another defeat for a Trump-backed candidate. The president hosted a tele-rally for Ogles just last week. Hatcher had the endorsement of Gov. Bill Lee. Second: This can be seen as a victory for the clean energy industry, which targeted Ogles with negative ads. Third: Ogles was routinely in the news for the wrong reasons, most notoriously drawing criticism from his fellow Republicans for a post that said, “Homosexuality has no place in America.” (He blamed a staffer.) But he was also rebuked by some Senate Republicans for Islamophobic rhetoric, which is a bit ironic given this next item coming up.

El-Sayed on his newly popular full name: “This is the best place in the world to be Abdul,” the freshly minted Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan — home to one of America’s largest Arab populations — told reporters this week. Republicans seem to think his name is a liability, NOTUS’ Angie Orellana Hernandez reports. Immediately after he was declared the primary winner, the NRSC sent out a press release referring to him as Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, rather than the name he’s used for his entire political career. It was a formulation the committee had not used previously.

Eyes on Hawaii: Another progressive vs. establishment battle is set for Saturday between state Democratic Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole and longtime Rep. Ed Case. Case, who has served seven nonconsecutive terms in Congress, is touting his seniority and ability as an appropriator to bring federal dollars home, NOTUS’ Christa Dutton tells us. Keohokalole’s pitch is that it’s time for change, especially after Case voted with Republicans on an early version of the SAVE Act and didn’t sign a letter with his fellow Hawaii Democrats condemning ICE raids.

Momentum is on Keohokalole’s side after progressive wins against incumbents in New York City and Denver, but Hawaii is an old-school Democratic state that isn’t quick to welcome change, said Colin Moore, a political scientist at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa. “Because progressive challenges to the Democratic establishment traditionally haven’t done all that well here, I think it would show that this anti-incumbency sense among the Democratic electorate is much broader than just very progressive Western or Northeastern areas,” Moore said.

From the White House


Another bite at birthright: With two new executive orders yesterday, the president made it clear he plans to continue trying to limit the constitutional rules around birthright citizenship, despite the Supreme Court decision earlier this year batting down his first attempt. NOTUS’ Manuela Silva details the new orders, one of which claims powers to deny citizenship to some children born in the U.S. under certain circumstances, while the other directs federal officials to deny visas to travelers coming to the U.S. for “birth tourism.”

From the courts


A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to pay several nonprofits by today at noon Pacific Time for the legal services they provided to unaccompanied migrant children, NOTUS’ Jackie Llanos reports. The Office of Refugee Resettlement, tasked with the care of the children, had withheld millions in reimbursements for legal representation since December because the nonprofits declined to provide information about their minor clients to protect their privacy. The office just gave a new sole-source, $150 million contract to a small Texas firm.





NEW ON NOTUS

House Republican scandals lead to midterm déjà vu: In a previous midterm where historical trends were on their side, 2006, Democrats were able to make their blue wave splash a little further up the beach thanks to a slew of scandals by Republican lawmakers that made them vulnerable in otherwise safe seats. Our Paul Kane looks back at that cycle and compares it to this one in his latest for NOTUS. That déjà vu line came from the Cook Political Report’s Amy Walter, who said, “In both years: unpopular war, members mired in sex scandals.”

More: Rep. Julie Johnson Violated Transparency Law With Dozens of Late Stock Disclosures, by Dave Levinthal

DOJ Sued Over Trump Tax-Audit Immunity Deal, by Jenna Monnin

Some Visa Applicants Could Pay Up to $250K in Bonds to Overcome Denials, by Jenna Monnin





NOT US

  • Moderate Democrats Prepare for ‘War’ Against an Ascendant Left, by Shane Goldmacher for The New York Times
  • Bobby Pulido is sick and tired of apologizing, by Samuel Benson for Politico
  • Senate Republicans launch network of fake news sites, by Judd Legum for Popular Information

entries.title: Retiring Sen. Gary Peters Is Already Negotiating His Next Gig
entries.summary: The Michigan senator’s term ends early next year.
entries.content:
Sen. Gary Peters is slated to represent Michigan on Capitol Hill for another five months. He’s already eyeing new opportunities on the West Coast.

A Senate ethics document reviewed by NOTUS indicates that Peters, a two-term Senate Democrat who isn’t seeking reelection this year, is negotiating employment with the University of Southern California.

The negotiations began on June 3, according to the ethics document, which Peters signed the same day.

Peters’ office confirmed that the senator “is having conversations about potential opportunities once he completes his Senate term.”

“He is following all Senate rules regarding future employment opportunities,” the office told NOTUS in a statement. “There are no additional details to share at this time.”

Senate ethics rules in part mandate that senators “must avoid not only an actual conflict of interest, but also the appearance of a conflict between their duties to the Senate and the interests of the prospective employers with whom they are negotiating.”

Representatives for the University of Southern California did not respond to phone and email messages requesting comment.

It’s unclear what kind of job Peters is seeking with the university or where he’d be located.

In addition to its main campus in Los Angeles, the University of South California has a “Capital Campus” in Washington, D.C., with a mission to “accelerate our influence and impact, promote and develop strong leaders, and forge critical partnerships to address the nation’s most pressing issues and opportunities.

It also has a sizable government relations operation, which typically spends hundreds of thousands of dollars each year on federal-level lobbying efforts.

This year alone, the University of Southern California has lobbied several government agencies, Congress and the White House on a variety of topics, ranging from higher education policy to national security and defense research, according to federal records.

entries.title: Cassidy Says He Will Back Blanche, Paving Way for Confirmation
entries.summary: The Louisiana Republican was the deciding vote on President Trump's nominee to lead the Justice Department.
entries.content:
Louisiana Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy announced that he will support acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination to lead the Justice Department, handing him enough votes to confirm him as early as later today before the Senate leaves for the August break.

“All considered, I will vote for Mr. Blanche,” Cassidy said in a speech on the Senate floor.

Cassidy defended Blanche on a number of fronts. He noted that Blanche was not the decider of pardons given out to Jan. 6 rioters and that even when he gives advice, President Donald Trump does not have to listen.

He also dismissed the acrimonious history between him and Trump, who endorsed his opponent earlier this year in his Senate primary race after Cassidy voted to convict him of his actions after Jan. 6, 2021.

“This is not a referendum on President Trump. It is the decision regarding Mr. Blanche in very specific circumstances,” Cassidy said. “I’ll be criticized for this decision, what’s new? The people of Louisiana can be assured that I worked hard to understand the issue and to make the right decision.”

Cassidy noted that he and Blanche spoke numerous times throughout the confirmation process, having just got off the phone with him right before his speech.

The move comes hours after Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) announced her opposition to Blanche’s nomination.

Much like Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) earlier in the week, Murkowski faulted Blanche for green-lighting the settlement with President Donald Trump that spawned the $1.8 billion Justice Department fund and the immunity deal that would have shielded Trump from future IRS audits.

Both parts of the deal have drawn widespread derision among Senate Republicans. That prompted Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) to push for an in-writing agreement that nixes the “slush” fund, which would have provided settlements to the Trump allies and Jan. 6, 2021 rioters, and the scope of the immunity accord.

Murkowski cast doubt that the issue will go away after a potential confirmation.

“I am also keenly aware that the Department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund—which likely would have rewarded January 6 protesters—is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage,” Murkowski said. “Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds.”

“The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration,” she continued. “I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case.”

Murkowski also cited Blanche's handling of the files related to crimes committed by Jeffrey Epstein, statements he reportedly made to pro-life groups and the DOJ’s attempt to indict Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) over videos encouraging military members to resist unlawful orders.
entries.author: Al Weaver

entries.title: Back Home in D.C., Stefon Diggs Has His Sights Set on a Super Bowl
entries.summary: On his first day with the Commanders, the DMV native said he came back home to win.
entries.content:
Throughout his 12-year career, only two things have eluded Stefon Diggs.

The first was a chance to play for his hometown team. The second is a Super Bowl trophy, something he was 60 minutes away from obtaining with the Patriots last season.

After officially signing with the Commanders on Friday, the Gaithersburg, Maryland, native has achieved one of those goals — and he feels his new team can provide him with a chance to reach the other.

“At this stage in my career everybody knows what I want. I want to win, and I want to hold a trophy up,” Diggs said after a sweltering two-hour practice in Ashburn.

“So, what a better place to do it than back home?”

The arrival of Diggs, who totaled a team-high 85 receptions for 1,013 yards and four touchdowns for the AFC champions last year, put an end to an offseason of speculation about Washington’s receivers room. Diggs only participated in a handful of snaps during Friday’s practice, but in time he will presumably slot in next to starter Terry McLaurin.

Diggs said he’s long admired McLaurin from afar, and he got a good first impression from rookie Antonio Williams.

“Fourteen can hoop a little bit,” Diggs said, referring to Williams’ jersey number. “You know, young guys don't get a name in the beginning. Just call them by the number.”

The Commanders have said all offseason that they are constantly evaluating the roster and open to bringing in free agents when they feel they need more competition at a position. They recently added vets at cornerback (Rasul Douglas) and center (Trey Hill), and that trend continued Friday with the signing of Diggs.

While Diggs’ 9,032 receiving yards since 2018 (third-most among wide receivers) was a big reason Washington made the call, coach Dan Quinn said he was also impressed by the veteran’s leadership skills and professionalism.

“People speak to the work ethic, the practice ethic, and so those are some of the things I'm very much looking forward to seeing,” Quinn said about Diggs before his arrival. “That's who you are. It's not something that doesn't travel, and so we're excited to add that type of competitor to our group.”

Quinn added that the team was “comfortable” bringing Diggs in after was found not guilty of assaulting his private chef in May. Diggs is currently a party in two separate civil lawsuits.

While there have been multiple times in his career that cameras have caught Diggs being an emotional leader on the sideline — for better or worse — the receiver said that, at this point in his career, he prefers to show more than tell.

“I can say a bunch of hoopla, but I'd rather just go out there and hoop and show you why I did what I did, or kind of just communicate through the actions,” Diggs said.

Even at his advanced (football) age of 32, Diggs still has the capabilities to be a game-changer on the field. Of the 20 players with at least 1,000 receiving yards last season, Diggs was the oldest and only one of two players (with Denver’s Courtland Sutton) over the age of 30. He had the highest catch percentage (83.3%) in the league last season, according to Next Gen Stats.

The 2015 fifth-round pick out of Maryland said he woke up early every morning and worked out at least three times a day over the past few months, hoping to be prepared for the moment he joined a team.

“I wasn't really too concerned about the where,” Diggs said of his free agency. “It was just the when and how.”

The signing marks a full-circle moment for Diggs. He grew up a fan of the Commanders and said he had a chip on his shoulder when the team passed on him in the 2015 draft. While his motivations have changed over the years, he still believes he has that drive — and he hopes it will help him land the championship trophy he covets.

“So here I am back home, and I carry that same chip, but I'm a part of the team now,” Diggs said. “I got a lot of pride, and I try to put it to the side at times, but that chip is on the other side now.”

entries.title: Senate Passes Russia Sanctions Bill Championed By Lindsey Graham
entries.summary: The chamber passed the sweeping measure that also includes Iran sanctions ahead of its August recess.
entries.content:
The Senate passed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill that would give President Donald Trump new power to punish countries that buy Russian oil and gas.

The bill, which passed 86-11, would impose sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, banks, state-owned companies and shadow-fleet vessels. It would also authorize tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the five largest importers of Russian oil or gas and the five leading facilitators of Russian oil sanctions evasion. China and India will likely be among the countries that could be affected.

Despite the overwhelming support for the bill, it faced opposition from senators who backed stronger sanctions on Russia but said its tariff provisions gave Trump too much control over trade.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune agreed to hold a vote on a bipartisan amendment from Sens. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky) to limit that authority. But Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia) sought changes to the tariff language and held up an agreement to expedite the bill, forcing Senate leaders to negotiate a deal before the August recess.

Warnock ended his holdout after securing a commitment from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer that tariffs could not remain in place if a country no longer qualified as a top-five buyer of Russian energy or a facilitator of sanctions evasion. The agreement cleared the way for amendment votes and final passage. Warnock plans to enter Greer’s letter into the Senate record.

The Senate rejected the Paul amendment 32-64, preserving the tariff authority backed by the White House. Trump would retain the power to impose tariffs of up to 100% on nearly all goods from major buyers of Russian energy, not just the oil and gas they purchase from Moscow.

The final bill allows the president to waive any sanction, restriction or tariff. Before issuing a waiver, the president must certify in writing that it’s in the national interests of the U.S. and submit a report to Congress explaining the decision.

Some pro-Ukraine Democrats said the waiver was too broad and warned that Trump could set aside the penalties during talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The bill would also extend the Iran Sanctions Act through 2031. The law gives the president authority to penalize activity tied to Iran’s energy and weapons sectors.

Most of the bill would expire five years after enactment. The Iran sanctions extension would remain in place through the end of 2031.

The bill had stalled while Trump pursued talks with Putin and sought more control over the sanctions. It began moving after Sens. Lindsey Graham (R-South Carolina), Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut), Jeanne Shaheen (D-New Hampshire) and Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) reached a White House deal that cut the proposed tariffs on Russian energy buyers from 500% to 100%, narrowed their reach and added the national-interest waiver.

The effort gained momentum after Graham’s death. Senators advanced the bill in an 86-12 procedural vote hours after his funeral, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy watching from the Senate gallery after meeting with lawmakers.

The bill was named for Graham, who had spent more than a year building support for it with Blumenthal.

Ahead of the vote, supporters were trying to head off amendments that could unravel the painstakingly crafted deal for Trump’s support as part of negotiations to ensure the bill would make it to the Senate floor for a vote.

The bill now faces an uncertain path in the House, which is out until the end of August.

Supporters of an emerging companion bill in the House have expressed confidence it would pass. That bill would be identical to the Senate-passed bill and would be introduced this week with solid Republican backing, according to a person familiar with the negotiations who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private deliberations.

That bill was on track this week, the person said, to have eight Republican co-sponsors and eight Democratic sponsors, including Reps. Steny Hoyer of Maryland and Marcy Kaptur of Ohio.

Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has said he wouldn’t support “handing President Trump a Trojan horse for tariff authorities he has repeatedly abused,” but the lawmaker said he remained “open to negotiating a good faith compromise.”

In June, the House passed a separate measure, sponsored by Meeks, that paired Russia sanctions with new aid and loans for Ukraine. It sanctions parts of the Russian economy but does not give Trump the same tariff authority as the Senate bill. The Senate does not plan to take up the measure because it lacks White House backing and drew limited Republican support.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi, Joe Gould

entries.title: The Finance Industry’s Workforce Appears to Be Feeling the Impacts of AI
entries.summary: New job numbers show major losses in a sector that’s led industries in adopting artificial intelligence.
entries.content:
The finance industry continues to be hemorrhaging jobs — and artificial intelligence could be partly to blame.

The financial activities sector, spanning finance, insurance and real estate industries, has lost 121,000 jobs since peaking in May 2025, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics report released on Friday. The latest numbers raise the possibility that the industry’s job market is contracting as AI is increasingly adopted.

“It stands to reason, at least some of it is due to AI,” said Ryan Young, a senior economist at the libertarian think tank Competitive Enterprise Institute. “AIs can do a lot of the grunt work that a lot of finance quants are doing right now, but humans still have to think of what questions to ask those models. They have to interpret what those models say, make decisions based on those.”

Financial firms have for years predicted AI would reduce their need for operations and technology staff, and increase roles in governance and compliance. Banks have outfitted their employees with AI training to boost productivity and invested tremendous amounts in the rapidly proliferating tech.

Those developments could now be spelling job cuts and slowed hiring.

Financial activities shed 14,000 jobs in July and hiring declined in the two months prior, though job openings shot up in June, the most recently available shows.

The sector lost 9,000 jobs alone last month in the field of credit intermediation, which lends funds to individuals and businesses. Those jobs span customer service representatives and bank tellers to mortgage loan officers and financial managers.

The losses could be a signal that borrowing in some areas is slowing down, as the market increasingly anticipates the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates this year. The central bank is staring down persistent inflation, which is creeping up as President Donald Trump’s prolonged war in Iran raises oil prices and throws the economy’s near-term future into uncertainty. Price pressures from Trump’s tariff policies worsen the problem.

Credit intermediation workers may face further labor market contractions.

If the Fed increases rates to tamp down inflation, borrowing will become more expensive for financial institutions and Americans looking for a home or credit loan.

Lending to private credit borrowers has already fallen sharply this year. Mortgage lending rates, which have been on an upward trend for most of this year, increased over the last month, according to data from Freddie Mac.

The jobs report released Friday counted job losses totaling 23,000 in July, compared to an average monthly gain of 34,000 in the last year. It further revised June numbers from 57,000 to 20,000 jobs added. The unemployment rate ticked down by a tenth of a percentage point to 4.1%.

The financial sector was not the only industry to experience job losses. Local government education lost 50,000 jobs and retail trade leaked 19,000 jobs, while health care continued adding jobs.
entries.author: Jade Lozada

entries.title: D.C. Wins Fight Against Trump Administration Over Voter Rolls
entries.summary: A federal judge dismissed the DOJ lawsuit, marking another defeat in the administration’s attempts to scour state records.
entries.content:
A federal judge on Thursday dismissed a lawsuit filed by the U.S. Department of Justice seeking a full, unredacted copy of D.C.’s voter registration data, marking another defeat for the Trump administration in its aggressive attempts to scour states’ voter rolls over claims of fraud and undocumented immigrants casting ballots.

In a 23-page ruling, U.S. District Court Judge Randolph D. Moss rejected the department’s attempt to use a 1960s-era civil rights law as part of what he called an “unprecedented effort to collect sensitive information about voters.”

The legal fight started more than a year ago, when the Department of Justice requested a full copy of D.C.’s voter registration list, including voters’ full names, dates of birth, addresses and either driver’s license numbers or the last four digits of their Social Security numbers.

The department said the request — which was made in virtually every state — was part of a broader effort to ensure that states were properly maintaining their voter rolls and removing ineligible voters.

But critics, including the left-leaning Brennan Center for Justice, called the push an “unprecedented and clear encroachment on states’ power to run elections” and “part of the administration’s concerted campaign to interfere with future elections.”

D.C. election officials turned over only a limited voter list, arguing that privacy laws precluded them from producing personally identifiable information like driver’s license or Social Security numbers.

In December 2025, the DOJ sued D.C. for its refusal to give up the information the department was seeking; similar lawsuits were filed against 30 states. Thus far, 21 judges have ruled against the requests.

“Having never won a case so far, with rebukes from judges all over, it’s time for the Department of Justice to drop its attempts to grab voters’ sensitive non-public data as part of a larger unlawful scheme to take over election administration, which our Constitution and federal laws wisely entrust to the states,” said Maryam Jazini Dorcheh, the vice president of litigation for watchdog group Common Cause.

The District’s election system and laws have come under repeated attack from Republicans in recent years, with some criticizing the city for allowing same-day voter registration, sending every voter a ballot in the mail, counting late-arriving mail ballots, implementing ranked-choice voting and permitting noncitizens to vote in local elections.
entries.author: Martin Austermuhle

entries.title: Trump Must Stop Ballroom Construction, Appeals Court Rules
entries.summary: The president said the administration will appeal the case to the Supreme Court.
entries.content:
A federal appeals court blocked construction on Donald Trump’s new White House ballroom on Friday, saying the president has no constitutional authority over the property “owned by the American people and stewarded by the National Park Service.”

The court’s 2-1 decision upheld a federal judge’s ruling in April that demanded construction stop until the administration received approval from Congress. The Trump administration could still decide to appeal the decision to the Supreme Court in the next two weeks before the order takes effect.

Trump said his administration would be immediately appealing to the Supreme Court in a Truth Social post hours after the decision was handed down, saying the court had failed to acknowledge the ballroom was "desperately needed.”

“This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy,” judges Patricia A. Millett and Bradley N. Garcia wrote in their majority opinion. “This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom. What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court’s expeditious litigation without securing Congress’s authorization, as the Constitution and laws require.”

Trump began demolishing the White House’s East Wing in October, despite previously pledging that the construction of his ballroom would not "interfere" with the previously standing building. Originally slated to cost $200 million — which the administration had said would come from private donors — The Washington Post reported in June that the actual bill could end up being closer to $600 million, with taxpayers potentially footing half of that bill.

“We are aware of no instance in American history in which a President unilaterally and using privately collected funds demolished substantial portions of the White House that Congress authorized to be built and American taxpayers paid for,” the majority wrote. “Until now.”

Judge Neomi Rao wrote that the preliminary injunction constituted a “clear abuse of discretion” in her dissent.

“This case is not about tearing down the White House and building a skyscraper or razing the Statue of Liberty,” Rao, a Trump appointee, wrote. “The equitable balance is between the asserted aesthetic harm to a single passerby and the safety and security of the President as well as his family, staff, and guests at the White House.”

In his Friday post, Trump praised Rao’s dissent and reiterated that the ballroom would not generate taxpayer expenses.

The “totally secure Ballroom, which is being built ahead of schedule and under budget, is a Gift from President Trump and Great Patriots of the United States of America,” he wrote.

This story was updated to reflect Trump's announcement.
entries.author: Manuela Silva

entries.title: Trump Revives Attempt to Oust Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook
entries.summary: The White House’s letter comes soon after the Supreme Court struck down an earlier effort on procedural grounds.
entries.content:
The Trump administration renewed its effort to fire Lisa Cook, the Federal Reserve governor he tried to remove last year before the Supreme Court blocked her ousting on procedural grounds.

In a White House letter dated Aug. 5 and signed by deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino, Cook was given 21 days to respond to allegations of mortgage fraud, claims Cook has repeatedly denied and for which she has not been criminally charged.

President Donald Trump tried to fire Cook last August, citing those unproven allegations. The Supreme Court said in October that she could not be removed from her position as the case played out. In June, the justices issued a 5-4 ruling siding with Cook, saying she was owed notice and a chance to respond to the allegations before being fired “for cause.” The court did not rule on the merits of the allegations surrounding her firing — effectively leaving the door open for the administration to attempt to remove her again.

The letter referenced the court’s decision when demanding a written explanation for “false statements” made on her mortgage agreements, saying Cook has had over 10 months and “ample opportunity to do so.”

“Nevertheless, the Supreme Court recently determined that you are entitled to notice of the allegations against you and an opportunity to respond prior to your removal,” the letter says after detailing several allegations related to mortgage fraud. “This is your opportunity to respond.”

Appointed by former President Joe Biden, Cook is the first Black woman to serve on the Federal Reserve Board of Governors. Currently, three Trump appointees sit on the seven-person board, and the president has repeatedly expressed a desire to have a “majority.”

In the Supreme Court’s decision, Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in a footnote that nothing stops the president from “trying again” to fire the governor — only that she must be given due process. Trump signaled he would take “appropriate action immediately” in a Truth Social post following the ruling, saying the decision was made “on a strictly procedural basis.”
entries.author: Manuela Silva

entries.title: ‘Between Perfection and Mr. Blanche’
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for Aug. 7, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Todd Blanche won last-minute support from retiring Sen. Bill Cassidy, who gave a morning floor speech before an eventual confirmation vote, which has not yet been scheduled.

  • “Mr. Blanche is not perfect,” the Louisiana Republican said, “but the choice is not between perfection and Mr. Blanche. It is between Mr. Blanche and another acting attorney general who may not run the department effectively under President Trump.”
The Senate passed its sweeping Russia sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham in an 86-11 vote. The measure faces an uphill battle in the House.

  • The chamber also cleared 74 additional nominations, including FEMA head Cameron Hamilton and TSA administrator David Cummins.
As of publication time, Senate leaders are still working on a deal to expedite passage of several pre-recess priorities, including a stopgap government funding bill and Blanche’s nomination. The Senate’s college sports bill has multiple GOP holdouts that could force it to slip into September.

  • “As you all know around here, people start getting more real about their demands as the clock rolls on,” John Thune said.




THE ADMINISTRATION

Donald Trump’s administration plans to ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on his ballroom — which he calls a “Military Center” — after a federal appeals court demanded he cease construction this morning.

Trump nominated Danielle Thumann, currently senior counsel to FCC Chair Brendan Carr, to serve as an agency commissioner. The panel comprises two Republicans and one Democrat.

The White House sent Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook a letter, signed by deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino, saying it was “considering” removing her from the position. SCOTUS’s June decision on her firing left an opening for Trump to revive his attempts.

The finance industry continues to hemorrhage jobs — and AI could be partly to blame, according to today’s Bureau of Labor Statistics report. Overall, the economy lost 23,000 jobs last month.





THE HILL

Retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Michigan) is already eyeing his next gig on the West Coast.

The White House sent a memo dispelling the notion that the Senate’s Protect College Sports Act could preempt state laws banning transgender women in women’s sports — an emerging GOP concern, Punchbowl reports.





THE STATES

The operator behind Trump-backed gas stations racked up nearly 200 penalties in New Jersey before Trump touted the network last month, Politico reports.

Maryland Republicans are suing after Democrats passed a ballot question concerning state redistricting earlier this week.





PRONOUNCED ‘AWE’

https://x.com/adamwren/status/2085805571907670087




Thank you for reading! Today’s newsletter was produced by Kelly Poe and Erik Schutz. If you like it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please subscribe — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at finalnotus@notus.com.

Correction: Yesterday’s newsletter misstated which state Sen. Boozman serves. He is a senator from Arkansas.

entries.title: Senate Punts Crypto Bill, But Regulation Fight Likely Before Midterms
entries.summary: The debate over the industry’s future will play out in the midterms, where campaign donations are mostly expected to benefit Republicans.
entries.content:
The Senate punted a vote on cryptocurrency legislation until after its five-week summer recess, increasing the odds that Congress will fail to regulate a growing market impacting the U.S. economy.

The bill, known as the CLARITY Act, is backed by many crypto interests, and was approved in a bipartisan vote by the House more than a year ago. The legislation would establish a framework for regulating cryptocurrencies, making it easier for digital assets to integrate with the existing U.S. financial system.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina), one of the key negotiators on the legislation, told reporters on Friday that the bill’s prospects “probably dropped 50%,” after it was kicked to September.

Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyoming), who led negotiations on the bill, which overhauls a wide range of federal financial regulations to incorporate crypto trading, repeatedly called for a vote on the measure ahead of the August recess.

“We’ve added 300 pages to the bill, it’s doubled in size, we’ve given [Democrats] 100 amendments they wanted,” Lummis said. “It’s time to vote. They were never serious about the 11 months that we put into this.”

But Senate Democrats continue to oppose the bill because they say it fails to adequately limit federal officials from investing in crypto.

Democrats rejected the ethics provision presented in the most recent draft of the bill. That language banned some officials from all three branches of government from issuing, sponsoring or promoting new digital assets while in office but did not require they fully divest from cryptocurrency and limited enforcement to the Department of Justice. Democrats have pushed for state attorneys general to have a role in enforcing those restrictions. The White House has been involved in months of negotiations over the broader bill and the ethics provision.

A bipartisan group of senators worked to write stricter ethics guardrails but are still in talks with the White House, which will now shift into the fall. Democrats are concerned about President Donald Trump and his family’s stake in World Liberty Financial, a decentralized finance platform and stablecoin issuer that’s expected to receive a federal banking charter soon.

Trump’s most recent financial disclosure shows he made more than $1 billion in crypto earnings in 2025.

“There's no bill, so far as I can tell. There is still no agreement that would prevent Donald Trump from making his next 1.4 billion dollars on crypto scams,” Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking committee, said.

Sens. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland) and Ruben Gallego (D-Arizona) joined Republicans to vote to advance the bill out of committee in May and have been involved in the negotiations around new restrictions. But both lawmakers said they will not support the bill on the Senate floor without a concrete ethics rule.

Alsobrooks said after a vote was postponed that talks will continue over the ethics provision and Democrats are still interested in “getting the CLARITY Act right.”

“It is so critical that we consider ethics; it’s what the American people expect of us,” Alsobrooks said. “We need this regulation to happen, so I support innovation and we have to have the kind of guardrails to make sure that we grow it responsibly.”

Democrats and an increasing number of Republicans have also expressed concerns about other parts of the legislation, including the crypto market’s impact on community banks and parts of the bill that absolve the businesses behind decentralized crypto platforms from having systems to stop money-laundering and other crimes.

The crypto industry had wanted Senate leadership to hold at least a procedural vote on the measure before the August recess in order to help direct some of its political spending ahead of the November elections, according to reporting by Semafor.

Fairshake, the leading crypto-aligned PAC, started the cycle with nearly $200 million cash on hand. But with Democrats blocking the legislation over the ethics provision, it’s unclear how crypto-affiliated groups might redirect their political spending.

“It's probably a good guess that the money will go primarily to Republicans, but it'll for sure go to pro-crypto candidates,” a source in the crypto industry who requested anonymity to discuss political talks told NOTUS, noting that cryptocurrency groups supported Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) and Gallego in their Senate bids.

The bill requires 60 votes to advance through the Senate, mandating some bipartisan support. Crypto-affiliated groups spent around $40 million to beat former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) in 2024 and are expected to spend heavily in this year’s Ohio, Michigan and Alabama Senate races and in other races across the country. Brown is challenging Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) in his bid to return to the Senate this year.

“If [crypto-affiliated super PACs] get stuffed by the Senate, I think they'll be, you know, I think all of those folks will have kind of gotten their answer as to who's with them and who's not in the midterms,” the source said.

Alsobrooks told NOTUS that Democrats have been working on crypto regulation all year and are not the ones blocking negotiations.

“Democrats have worked hard,” Alsobrooks said when asked if she is concerned about the possibility of crypto political donations benefiting Republicans. “If it fails because of ethics, it's going to be because Republicans refused to take on this president and to put the kind of guardrails in place that American people demand.”

Sen. Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, echoed Alsobrooks, telling NOTUS that Democrats can’t settle for a bill that does not adequately regulate the industry in order to secure political donations.

“I think it is masquerading as legislation,” King said. “I'm just concerned that it's a terrible piece of legislation that would be bad for the country and national security.”
entries.author: Avani Kalra
